verifier_reason: test_outputs.py::test_jump_analyzer_test_video: The test failed in the call phase due to an assertion error

items.name: Readability
items.evidence: There are no docstrings on analyze_video or main. Some names are cryptic: single-letter `M`, `ym`, `t`, `lbl`, `fi`. There are a few helpful comments ("Walk backwards from t_peak..."), but thresholds like `y_peak + 60` and `- 12` are never explained.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: analyze_video is about 135 lines (over the 100-line cap). It does frame extraction, stabilization, segmentation and takeoff/landing search in one function, against the convention of separate functions. The backward and forward plateau walks are copy-pasted. main also has hand-rolled argument parsing.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: There is no `cap.isOpened()` check. When nothing is detected, `return 0, 0` quietly produces fake output. There are many unnamed magic constants: `> 28`, `>= 15`, `>= 300`, `180`, `>= 200`, `w * 0.32`, `+ 60`, `- 12`, `t_peak + 4`. Output files are written without any error handling.

items.name: Robust to bad inputs and missing detections
items.name_zh: 异常输入与检测失败的处理
items.evidence: The video is never checked as opened. An empty video or no detection gives `return 0, 0`, which is written as 0/0 with exit code 0. Thresholds are fixed pixel values tuned on the example (diff > 28, area >= 300, hurdle zone 0.32w–0.72w), and the hidden test failed.

items.name: Output contract honoured
items.evidence: Takes the first positional arg as the video and writes /app/output.toml with exactly the two int fields. Without an argument it quietly falls back to the hard-coded `/app/example_video.mp4`, and it accepts extra output paths. It never states that frames are 0-based.
